# The Sitting

She arrived younger than he had expected, and considerably more innocent. When she appeared at his door, presenting herself in response to the advertisement he had posted, he felt a small pang of disappointment. He had hoped for someone with a harder edge—a face that carried some visible weight of experience, some complication in the eyes. Instead, she stood before him fresh and untroubled, as though the world had not yet found reason to mark her.

Yet appearances, he knew, could mislead. As she settled in and drew off her gloves, he noticed the pale gleam of a wedding band. She pulled photographs from her purse without prompting—small faces, children—and in that instant the illusion shifted. Despite her youthful, almost virginal air, she was a mother. The knowledge rearranged her in his mind, lending her a quiet gravity he had not perceived a moment before.

He guided her toward the old garden chair positioned near the window. It was a worn and unremarkable thing to any other eye, but to him it held a deep and private significance, its faded wood bound up with memories he rarely spoke aloud. He arranged her within it carefully, as though placing something fragile inside a reliquary.

Then the light bulb overhead began to sway.

He could not have said what set it moving—a draft, perhaps, or the tremor of his own hand against the cord—but the slow, pendular swing of it caught him and pulled him backward through the years. Suddenly he was no longer in his studio. He was inside the medical tent again, its canvas walls straining, the air thick with the sound of wounded men. The moaning rose around him from every side, low and ceaseless, a chorus of the broken.

Beyond the tent, the enemy's weapons shrieked in the distance, each cry drawing nearer or falling away in a rhythm he had learned to dread. And the smells returned with terrible fidelity: the sharp sting of ether, the sterile weight of gauze, the copper undertone of blood. In those days he had been made to sketch the injured—to render the exposed tissue, the ruined limbs, the raw geography of suffering—and the sensory assault had so overwhelmed him that his pencil would tremble uselessly above the page, unable to move.

He stood now in the quiet studio, the young mother waiting patiently in the chair, the bulb still swinging above them both, and he understood that some sittings summon more than a likeness.

# Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida

She comes to me on a Tuesday, still smelling of the street—of rain and cheap powder and the nervous sweetness of youth that hasn't yet learned to distrust itself. I set the chair for her near the window, the old garden chair with its wickerwork gone soft and gray, the one I dragged in from beneath the eaves years ago because I liked how it held the memory of weather. "Sit," I tell her, and she does, arranging her hands in her lap the way girls do when they think stillness is the same as grace.

Ida. That is the name I have given her, though I do not know if it is hers. It hardly matters. A model becomes whatever the canvas requires, and the canvas requires a soul—a soul newly arrived, blinking, unfinished, the paint of the world not yet dry upon her.

I begin with the light. I always begin with the light, because light is the first cruelty. It falls across her shoulder and I watch it pool in the hollow of her throat, and for a moment—only a moment—the lamp above her seems to swing.

It is the tents I remember then. It is always the tents.

I had been a young man too, in France, drawing the wounds of soldiers so the surgeons might study them. Medical illustration, they called it, as though there were anything medical about the way a lamp swung on its hook above a cot and threw a boy's ruined face into gold and then into shadow and then into gold again. I learned the human body there. Not as the anatomists teach it, clean and Latin and abstract, but as it truly is: perishable, weeping, held together by nothing more than habit and the mercy of the hour. I learned that skin is not a surface but a record. That every vein is a small river carrying its cargo toward some inevitable sea. That flesh remembers everything the mind tries to forget.

So now, when I look at Ida—at this smooth, unmarked girl of nineteen or twenty who has never been sick a day in her life—I cannot help it. My brush finds the lamp swinging. My brush finds the years that have not yet touched her and paints them anyway. I thicken her ankles. I mottle her hands. I let time collect in the folds of her dress and the loose flesh of her arm, all the ruin that is coming, all the ruin I saw come to those boys before they were even old enough to earn it.

"Am I so terrible?" she asks once, half-laughing, when she steals a glance at the canvas. She does not understand. It is not terror I am painting. It is truth, which is a kinder and more unbearable thing.

For this is what I know that she does not: a soul does not arrive into the world all at once, whole and shining. It arrives the way the wounded arrived in those tents—carried, uncertain, already marked by the journey. It comes into the light only to be measured by the darkness waiting at the edge of the lamp's swing. And the work of the painter, like the work of the boy I was, is only to keep watch. To record. To say, *here, this happened, this was flesh, this was alive, and I saw it.*

The lamp above her steadies. The room is only a room again. Ida shifts in the old garden chair and sighs, and outside the rain goes on falling on a city full of souls newly come, none of them knowing yet what the light will make of them.

I mix a little green into the shadow of her cheek. I begin again.

# After Ivan Albright

Ivan Albright (1897–1983) remains one of the most singular figures in American art, a painter whose meticulous depictions of decay, mortality, and the passage of time continue to captivate and unsettle viewers long after his death. To look at his work is to confront the relentless truth of aging—each wrinkle, blemish, and shadow rendered with an almost obsessive precision.

## A Painter of Time

What sets Albright apart is his fascination with the effects that come *after*—after youth has faded, after flesh has begun to sag, after life has left its mark on every surface. His paintings are studies in aftermath, capturing not the bloom of vitality but the slow, inevitable erosion that follows. Objects, faces, and hands appear weathered and worn, as though time itself had been the true collaborator on each canvas.

His most famous contribution to popular culture came through cinema: Albright created the grotesque portrait for the 1945 film adaptation of *The Picture of Dorian Gray*. The image, depicting the corruption of Dorian's soul, perfectly embodied Albright's lifelong themes—the visible consequences of sin, vanity, and the erosion of the body.

## Technique and Obsession

Albright worked with extraordinary slowness, sometimes spending years on a single painting. He built elaborate still-life environments in his studio, controlling light and composition with scientific rigor. His palette leaned toward greens, purples, and earthy tones, creating an atmosphere of luminous decay.

Working after the traditions of realism yet distinct from any movement, Albright forged what critics have called "magic realism"—an unflinching vision that transforms the mundane into the profound.

## A Lasting Legacy

Today, works by Ivan Albright hang in major institutions, reminding us that beauty and horror often occupy the same frame. His art endures as a meditation on what remains after everything else has passed away.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of creative fiction inspired by Ivan Albright's painting "Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida," imagining the artist and his model.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Seeing

The girl was twenty when she first climbed the stairs to Albright's studio, and she thought herself beautiful, which she was.

Her name was Ida Rogers. She had answered the notice for a model expecting the usual work—holding a pose while some earnest painter flattered her into an approximation of herself, all soft edges and golden light. She had modeled before. She knew how it went. The men always made you lovelier than you were, and you left feeling you'd been seen, even if what they saw was a lie.

Ivan Albright did not flatter.

"Sit," he said, and gestured to a chair beside a small round table. He arranged a powder puff in her hand, a mirror on the table, coins scattered as if she'd been counting her worth. He draped her in a dress the color of dried roses and told her to look into the glass.

Then he began to look at her himself.

She had never been looked at like this. It was not desire—she knew desire, had felt it warm and clumsy from a dozen men. This was something colder and more total. He looked at her the way a physician looks at a wound, the way winter looks at a field. He looked at her for a very long time before he touched the canvas.

"You're going to make me pretty," she said, to break the silence.

He didn't smile. "I'm going to make you true."

---

The sittings went on for weeks, then months. He worked slowly, unbearably slowly, laying down layer after translucent layer of paint. She came to understand that he was not painting the surface of her but everything beneath it, and everything that was coming.

She saw the canvas only once, early, and did not ask to see it again.

The Ida in the painting was not twenty. She was ageless in the worst way—her flesh gone doughy and mottled, her young hand made heavy, the fingers thick and reddened as though she'd spent forty years in scalding dishwater. Her face sagged toward sorrow. Her legs, beneath the hem, were swollen. The powder puff in her hand seemed a pitiful thing, a small defense against a siege that had already been lost.

"That isn't me," she'd whispered.

"Not yet," he'd said.

---

She grew to hate him a little, and then, strangely, not at all.

Because Ivan Albright looked at his own hands the same way. She watched him once, resting between sessions, turning his palms over in the gray light from the north window, studying the blue rivers of vein beneath the skin as though reading a verdict. He looked at the apples in the bowl until they browned. He looked at the flowers until they dropped their petals, and then he painted the petals where they fell.

"Everything is dying," he told her, not cruelly. "The moment a thing is born it begins to go. The peach on the branch, the girl in the chair. I only paint what time is already doing. I paint slowly so I can see it happening."

"That's a terrible way to live," she said.

"It's the only honest way to see." He set down his palms. "Everyone else looks away. They paint the rose at noon and pretend there's no evening. I stay until dark. I paint the evening in."

---

There was a title he'd chosen, and he told it to her near the end.

*Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida.*

"A soul," she repeated. "Not a body."

"The body is the tragedy," he said. "The soul is what makes the tragedy matter. Anyone can mourn a rotting apple. But a soul—" He gestured toward the canvas, toward the sorrowing woman with the powder puff, mourning the loss of a beauty she could not yet know she'd lose. "A soul called Ida came into the world. That's the whole story. Everything else is just what the world does to her afterward."

She looked at the painting then, really looked, the way he had taught her to look without meaning to teach her anything. And she understood that he had not made her ugly.

He had made her *mortal*, which is a harder and more loving thing. He had looked at a beautiful young woman and refused to let her be only that, refused the easy lie of the eternal noon. He had seen the whole arc of her at once—the child she had been, the tired woman she would become, the soul that would carry both. He had loved her enough to tell the truth.

---

Ida Rogers lived a long life. She married, had children, grew old the way everyone grows old, slowly and then all at once. Decades later she would go to the museum in Chicago and stand before the painting, an old woman looking at a young woman who had been painted old.

By then she had caught up to it. Her hands had thickened. Her face had learned the same downward pull of gravity and grief.

And she found, to her surprise, that she was not afraid of the painting anymore, and had not been for a long time. The girl in the rose-colored dress was not a curse he'd laid on her. She was a companion who had waited, patiently, all these years, for Ida to arrive.

*Into the world there came a soul called Ida,* she thought, standing there among the strangers who glanced and moved on, unable to bear the looking.

She stayed. She had learned, from him, how to stay until dark.

She looked at the painting the way he had looked at her—completely, unflinchingly, with the terrible tenderness of someone who refuses to turn away.

And the soul called Ida looked back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

# After IVAN ALBRIGHT's *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*

He learned the body first as inventory. In the medical tents of France, twenty years old and drawing what the surgeons opened, he made portraits of the wound before the wound was closed—each severed thing rendered exact, so that later, elsewhere, a man might be reassembled from paper. This was his apprenticeship to ruin. He held the pencil the way others held morphine: something to steady the hand against what the hand had seen.

So when Ida sits, forty and made to look eighty, she is not cruelty. She is the same tenderness continued by other means. He gives her the hand mirror, the powder puff, the last hope of the mouth still reaching for its youth, and around her he builds the truth of tissue—the blued veins, the pooled and mottled flesh, the knee that has begun its slow negotiation with the grave. He paints as if flaying were a form of love. Every varicose river, every crepe fold at the throat, is drawn with the devotion of the boy who catalogued the dying, who understood that to see completely is the only mercy we can offer the perishable.

Look how long it took him. Months at a single square inch. He mixed the palette of decay: the greens of gangrene remembered, the yellows of jaundice, the violet bruise that blooms beneath translucent skin. His studio was another surgical theater, the model another soldier, and the war he could not stop refighting was the war that time wages on all soft matter. He would not lie. He had seen too much of the interior to flatter the exterior.

And yet—*Into the world there came a soul.* Not a corpse. A soul, arriving, housed in this failing architecture of meat and memory. The title is the whole argument. He is saying: even here, in the ruined tent of the flesh, the light gets in. Even the amputated held a self. Even Ida, sagging toward her ending, was a *coming*, a genesis, a soul that entered the world through this particular unrepeatable door of skin.

He spent his life proving that the horror and the holy are the same brushstroke, differently believed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ekphrastic short story about a painter examining a young woman who comes to model for him, weaving in his memories of being a medic during wartime.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sitting

The light comes from the north, as it must. Everything else in the studio can be arranged—the drape of the cloth, the angle of the chair, the girl herself—but the light is a fact, like weather, like death.

She sits where I have placed her, turned three-quarters toward the window, her hands folded in her lap. She does not know what to do with her hands. No one ever does. They imagine that stillness is easy, that a body can simply stop, but the body is always doing something, always pulsing with its small insistences.

"Lower your chin," I tell her. "Just slightly. Yes."

Her name is Eloise. She is perhaps twenty. There is a translucence to her that the young have and cannot know they have, a quality that photographs cannot capture because photographs are too honest. Paint lies better. Paint tells the truth by lying.

I mix the flesh tones on my palette—lead white, a touch of vermilion, yellow ochre, the faintest breath of terre verte for the shadows. The green beneath the pink. People are always surprised to learn that skin is green in its recesses, in the hollow of the throat, along the underside of the jaw. But I have seen skin in every register. I know its full chromatic range.

She has a small vein at her temple. I watch it.

---

There was a boy at Verdun with a vein like that. We called it the aid station though it was a cellar, a stone room where we brought them by lantern light and they became, in that yellow glow, almost beautiful. I was nineteen and I had wanted to be a painter and instead I had become a student of anatomy in the worst possible school.

The boy's name I never knew. He had been opened along the abdomen and there was nothing to be done except the thing we did, which was to make the dying easier if we could. I held his hand. His temple had a vein that fluttered like Eloise's flutters now, and I watched it, because I could not watch his eyes.

The color of him. That is what returns to me. The gray-green of the truly cold, the marbling that comes, the way the lips go the color of old plums. I learned my palette there, in that cellar, though I did not know I was learning it. I thought I was only trying to survive the knowledge.

---

"Am I doing it right?" Eloise asks. Her voice is small.

"There is no right," I say. "Only hold what you have. You have it."

I begin with the underpainting, the ground of it, the architecture of shadow. The brush moves and I am not entirely present in the moving; the hand knows its business. I lay in the darkness first. Always the darkness first. You build toward the light, you earn it, stroke by stroke, and you cannot rush it or the whole thing turns to mud.

Her throat. The clavicle beneath the thin fabric. The living machinery of her, all of it working, all of it going about the invisible labor of keeping her here in the chair in the north light. I painted a man once who had lost his throat—no, I did not paint him, I dressed the ruin of his throat and he looked at me with such apology, as though he were sorry to be so much trouble, as though the shell that found him had been a small social embarrassment.

I have never told anyone this. I have put it into pigment instead. It is in every canvas I have made in forty years, buried under the flowers and the fruit and the pretty women, buried like the green beneath the pink.

---

The morning wears on. The light shifts, cools, and I must work faster now, chasing it.

"You're crying," Eloise says. She has broken the pose; she is looking at me. "Monsieur, you're crying."

I had not known. I touch my face and find that it is true.

"It's only the light," I tell her. "At my age the eyes water. Please—your chin, as it was."

She resumes the pose. She is kind enough to pretend to believe me. And I look at her again, this girl who was born decades after the cellar, after the lantern, after the boy whose hand I held while his vein went still—this girl who is made entirely of futures, who carries no green beneath her pink except the ordinary green of being alive.

I paint her that way. I give her all the light I withheld from myself. I let her be only what she is: young, and here, and not dying, not dying, gloriously and stubbornly not dying in the cold clean northern light.

It is the truest thing I have ever done. And she will never know what it cost, or what it saved, or that the two are the same thing, and always were.

"There," I say at last, when the light is gone. "We are finished."

But I do not put down the brush. Not yet. Not quite yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental narrative that shifts between third-person past (the artist) and first-person present (the model) about the making of Albright's Ida painting.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Looking

## I.

The artist mixed his colors slowly, the way a man might approach something he intended to wound. Ivan Albright had already spent three days on the hands alone, and the hands were not yet ready to be seen. He worked in the north light of the Warren Avenue studio, where the shadows collected like sediment in the corners and refused to leave.

---

I am sitting again. He has fixed the position with chalk on the floor—here for my heels, here for the chair's back legs—so that each morning I return to exactly the same fold of air I left the evening before. The mirror is angled so I can see myself if I want to. I do not want to.

My name is Ida. The name he gives the painting will be longer, will be a sentence almost, a joke that isn't funny. But this morning I am only Ida, and the light is coming up gray through the high windows, and my powder is already beginning to crack.

---

## II.

He had found her, or someone like her, and the distinction did not matter to the work. What mattered was the flesh—the way it pooled and gathered, the way time had made its slow accounting in the upper arms, the throat, the softening architecture of the jaw. Albright did not paint what he saw. He painted what he knew was coming for all of them, himself included, and he loved it the way an undertaker might love the exactness of his measurements.

The powder puff. He needed the powder puff in her hand, needed the futility of it, that small pink absurdity held against the tide.

---

I hold the puff the way he asks. My arm has fallen asleep and the sleep travels up into the shoulder, and I let it, because he has told me that the discomfort will be in the picture, that he can see it. I don't know if I believe him. But there is something in the way he refuses to flatter me that I have come to trust more than kindness.

Look at me, I want to say to whoever will stand before this someday. Look at what he has done. He has made me old past my age, made my skin the color of things left too long in water. But he has also *looked*. For eight hundred hours he has looked at me, and no one—not my husband, not my mother, not God—has ever looked at me so long.

---

## III.

The green came from nowhere in nature. He laid it into the shadows of her flesh, viridian and a bruised olive, because decay is not brown, decay is every color at once, refusing to be named. His brushes were small, absurdly small for the scale of his obsession. He worked one square inch at a time, and the inch would take a day, and the day would take something out of him he never bothered to name.

Two years he would keep at it. The dress against the chair. The mirror's dim reflection. The garter cutting into the thigh like a promise breaking.

---

Two years. I have grown genuinely older while he painted me growing older, so that at the end I have caught up to the woman on the canvas, or nearly. This is the joke I understand now, the one he could not have planned: that he was painting prophecy, and I have been walking slowly into the frame.

My feet hurt. The chair is hard. The powder settles into the lines around my mouth and he leans close, so close I can smell the linseed and the tobacco, and he says nothing, only looks, only carries some small truth of me back to the easel in his eyes.

I am not beautiful. I was never going to be beautiful in his hands.

But I am going to *last*.

---

## IV.

When it was finished he titled it against her: *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida.* As though she were only arriving. As though all that ruin were a beginning and not an end. Albright cleaned his impossible small brushes and stood back and felt what he always felt, which was nothing like satisfaction—only the cold completion of an argument he had been having with mortality since he was a boy in his father's studio, posing as a corpse.

The woman gathered her things. The chalk marks stayed on the floor for months, ghost-position, waiting.

---

I stand, finally, for the last time. The blood comes back into my legs like an accusation. I do not look at the painting on my way out; I have decided this in advance. Let others look. Looking was always his job and never mine.

At the door I pause. Outside, the ordinary afternoon is happening—streetcars, a man selling something, the plain unpainted world.

I step into it.

I am forty, or fifty, or the age he has made me. It no longer matters. Somewhere behind me a version of my face is learning how to outlive its own hands, and I am walking out under the actual sky, still warm, still moving, still—for a little while longer—more than a picture of myself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# The Backstory of Ida

*Ivan Albright's "Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida" (1929-1930)*

---

She came on a gray Tuesday, answering the notice the painter had posted—a model wanted, a few dollars for the sitting. Her name was Ida Rogers, and she was young then, barely twenty, though you would not know it from the canvas that would make her strange and immortal.

**Who she was:**

Ida had the ordinary hopes of an ordinary woman. She had married, perhaps too young. She kept house. She dreamed, quietly, the way people do when they haven't yet learned that dreams require a certain violence to fulfill. She came to Albright's studio because the money mattered, and because there was something flattering, at first, in the idea of being *seen*.

**Why she came:**

She thought she would be made beautiful. That is what portraits were for, in her understanding—to catch the best hour of a face and hold it against time's erosion. She sat expecting flattery.

**What the artist saw:**

But Albright was not painting Ida the woman. He was painting *time itself* as it lived within her. Beneath his obsessive brush, her young skin bloomed with premonition—every future sag and shadow, every vein and mortification the years would bring, summoned forward and laid upon her now. She sits half-dressed, powdering herself before a mirror we cannot see, mourning a beauty that is only beginning to leave her, or perhaps has not yet left at all.

The tragedy Albright saw was not ugliness. It was **vanity meeting mortality**—the human insistence on preserving what cannot be preserved. In Ida he found all of us: the soul that arrives in the world unasked, dresses itself in flesh, and spends its brief hours grieving the very body it was given.

He aged her decades in paint. When the real Ida saw herself, she is said to have wept.

---

*And yet: he loved her enough to look. That is the paradox of the portrait—that such unflinching attention is itself a kind of tenderness.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
